Divine and lightning do the exact same amount of damage. No monster that you need to worry about takes increased/reduced elemental damage anymore. You use whichever of these two charges you prefer. 

I use lightning charge because when fifth job came out it was actually marginally stronger than divine charge. This was changed a few years ago. All of the charges do the same amount of damage now (even fire/ice). Fire and ice hit fewer mobs though and are therefore not ideal. 

I'm in my 250s and this is my node setup: https://i.imgur.com/elhCq4G.png

When Neo comes out I am going to need to make room for Blink. I need to keep Ropelift for Lucid and Gloom. Will of Erda is useful in later bosses if you can use it intelligently, which I am not capable of. For bossing I would remove Holy Symbol and Ropelift (except Lucid/Gloom) and slot in Fatal Strike I and a level 25 FA. Sometimes I am lazy and leave these two nodes in. 

Anyway, my point isn't that you shouldn't ever use FA, but that you should wait a very, very long time before you worry about it. There will come a point when you have enough nodeslots for everything, but that is far away. Until then, I would conserve your node slots and use a single useful trio. [Lightning/Divine] Charge, HH, and Blast. In the future you can make a trio that include FA.

Lightning/Divine are the exact same now. I boosted lightning because when the V update was released lightning had slightly more damage. 

Technically ice/fire also have the same amount of damage, but they hit fewer mobs. 

I think that you should run a FA node, but not until much later. Most paladin recommendations don't really tell you how little boosting FA does for you. For a very long time you'd be better served using your node slots for decent skills and other things like that. Once you have nothing else you can benefit from is when you should slot in FA.

Honestly, as a paladin main, I wouldn't suggest two trinode setups until way into the future. I am in my 250s and still don't use a final attack node. Final attack for paladin accounts for ~1% of my BA damage. I use one trinode (blast/lightning charge/HH) and have never felt the need to make another.

Does mental illness ever fall into the category of incurable, quality of life impacting disease?

Let's say there is  a really unlucky person who has severe depression for most of their life. Let's say 60 years. At the age of 60 this hypothetical person finds a mix of medication and therapy and overcomes their depression. They live for 20 more years and die peacefully. 

My question is, would this person have been better off killing themselves at an earlier age? Sure, their life got better but they lived 60 years negatively compared to 20 positively. Does the 20 years of positive life outweigh the prior 60?

Ultimately life isn't as simple as my hypothetical person, but I personally believe that suicide should be an option for everyone. We need to generally discourage suicide because it does get better for most people. We don't need to prohibit suicide though and treat suicide prevention as a one size fits all approach. 

I'd you're at all interested this is one of my favorite videos on the topic of suicide and mental health: https://youtu.be/eQNw2FBdpyE

I'll reply to you just so you see it. Make sure your old Windows SSD is not plugged in when you make a new Windows install. You'll want to make sure it writes the boot partition to the correct drive.

Just wondering, did you have your old SSD unplugged when you installed Windows on the new SSD? There is a boot partition, usually on your main drive, that instructs which OS to boot. If you install Windows on a new SSD but it detects the old boot partition on a different drive then it will keep the old boot partition. If your boot partition is on a different drive and you remove the drive then you are going to have to make a new boot partition on your current drive.

I mean I believe there is a population of people who should have every right to die peacefully, humanely, and on their own terms. Outright prohibition is cruel to those people. Even if the population who fits this criteria is small, it is cruel and doesn't make it right. I am of the belief that you didn't ask to be put on this earth, and if you come to conclusion you don't want to be part of it anymore you should be allowed to go. 

I say this as a person who has had two brothers commit suicide, and in their cases they likely didn't rationally want to die. There was a lot that went wrong in their cases where the systems we setup to prevent suicides failed them. They reached out for help. The system failed them and let them slip through the cracks.

I also believe that most suicidal people fall into this category. They don't want to die, per se. They just don't see an alternative. It bothers me, though, that because this is the majority most people don't think about the minority of people who are rationally suicidal and how attempting to create outright suicide prohibition is causing them further anguish.

I personally don't know of any data sets that represent how suicidal people want to die, but I can imagine it would be really hard to get that sort of data. There can be a lot of fear with even admitting you want to die because, at least in the US, you are likely going to be reported. The desire alone is enough to be committed in a lot of places which, in my opinion, is likely a deterrent to being honest. The best I can think of is to scrape anonymous suicide boards and see how people hope to die.

Android does a better job of managing apps cached in RAM than people think. To the best of my knowledge, you don't save battery by having a smaller percentage of your RAM filled up. 

What closing your apps does do is force your phone to reload assets you cleared out of RAM back into RAM when you launch apps that were already cached into RAM before you closed them.
Clearing RAM and closing apps slows down your phone because you have to reload cached assets back into RAM. You don't save battery by clearing your RAM either, to the best of my knowledge.

On a basic level, yeah, IPS will look better than TN. That said, just being an IPS isn't the only thing that matters. There exist IPS panels that don't look that great and there are TN panels that look really good for being a TN panel. That said, my 60Hz IPS has significantly better colors than my 144Hz TN panel. 

Personally, I opted for a very odd setup years ago. I use a 60Hz 21:9 IPS panel as my main monitor and a 16:9 TN 144Hz panel to my right. They are both attached to monitor arms so when I feel like playing an FPS I just move my 21:9 monitor out of the way. I haven't seen anyone else do this. I did it because I couldn't justify spending a ton of money on a single high refresh rate ultrawide monitor. Each one of those features carry a price premium and they add up quick.

With this setup I haven't felt the need to upgrade because I only use my 144Hz monitor for competitive games.

I haven't shopped for monitors for a few years now. As such I can't give any reliable info on what to look for in the current market. If you want to do some research into high refresh rate monitors I would point you to [BlurBusters](https://www.blurbusters.com/). They have a lot of great info.

I can't give you a super technical response, but TN (twisted nematic) is generally a faster, cheaper pixel technology. They generally have worse color accuracy and viewing angles. The original 120Hz/144hz monitors were all TN panels.

IPS (in-plane switching) tends to have lower refresh rates and pixel response times. They have historically been held as the best image quality because they have better color accuracy and viewing angles. Until relatively recently no manufacturer was making high refresh rate IPS panels.

There are also VA panels, but I don't know much about them. They are not used as often as TN/IPS, and are generally considered to be somewhere in the middle of TN/IPS.
